text: By default, a process inside a container runs as root -- the same root the kernel recognizes on the host. If an attacker breaks out of that container, they're already most of the way to compromising the host itself.

USER node switches the container off root, onto the non-root user the official Node image already includes for exactly this. The chown flag on the copy matters too -- without it, those files would still be owned by root, unreadable by the user you just switched to.

Read-only makes the filesystem read-only outside of mounted volumes and tmpfs, so a compromised process can't rewrite the app's own code. Cap-drop-all strips every one of the roughly forty Linux capabilities bundled into root, and cap-add adds back only the single one actually needed -- here, binding a privileged port.

A full ubuntu image ships a package manager and a shell -- more for an attacker to work with after a compromise. A slim image has far fewer packages. Distroless or scratch has no shell and no package manager at all -- barely anything to pivot to, even with code execution.

None of this prevents every attack, but it shrinks what's available after one succeeds. That's the last piece of production hardening in this course -- next, why Compose itself stops working past one host, and a look at what comes after it.
